h1: The 6 Best Google TVs of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six Google TV sets from TCL and Hisense, from 55 to 85 inches, with refresh rates, panel types and who each one suits.
summary: The TCL 65 inch QM8K is the best Google TV for most households, balancing size and a 120Hz QLED panel. The QM8L steps up to 75 inches and 144Hz, while the Hisense U7 offers 165Hz in 55 and 85 inch sizes. The CanvasTV is a style choice, and the QM6K is the lower-series 75 inch.
intro: Google TV is the same software on every set in this ranking, so the platform cannot be your tie-breaker. The choice comes down to hardware that differs between TCL and Hisense: how big the screen is for your couch distance, how fast the panel refreshes, and which backlight sits behind the glass. Buyers who treat the operating system as the deciding feature end up comparing menus that are identical.

We reviewed six models from TCL and Hisense and ranked them on paper using size, refresh rate and panel type. The listings here give limited detail, so brightness, HDMI configuration and local dimming are unranked. Check those on the maker's page, and be skeptical of any spec line that contradicts a model's own title.

products.name: TCL 65 Inch Class QM8K Series
products.verdict: The most balanced size and spec mix in this group.
products.description:
The QM8K is a 65 inch QLED TV with a 120Hz panel running Google TV, in the $500 and up bucket. A 120Hz panel matters for two sources in particular: sports, where fast panning looks smoother, and current game consoles, which can output at that rate. QLED adds a quantum dot layer for a wider color range than a plain LED set.

It leads because 65 inches suits the usual couch distance in a living room, and 120Hz covers nearly everything a household watches. The QM8L adds a faster panel but also takes more wall.

It is a sensible default for a typical couch distance. The caveat is that the listing gives few other specs, so check the product page for HDMI details before you commit, especially if you own a console.
products.skipIf: You want a very large screen.

products.name: TCL 75 Inch Class QM8L Series
products.verdict: A bigger screen with a 144Hz panel.
products.description:
The QM8L is a 75 inch QLED set with a 144Hz panel, in the $500 and up bucket. It steps up both size and refresh rate over the QM8K, and the faster panel matters if a gaming PC feeds the screen, since PC games often render beyond 120 frames per second.

It follows closely, but the trade is room. Seventy-five inches wants a longer sofa distance, and a 144Hz panel only helps with sources that actually send that rate. Movies and streaming run far slower, so for most viewing the QM8K does the same job in a smaller footprint.

Pick it for a big room and a gaming PC or console that can use 144Hz. Otherwise 120Hz is plenty. Skip it if your wall is small, and check the stand width against your furniture before ordering.

products.name: Hisense 55" U7 Mini-LED ULED 4K UHD Best Premium Gaming Google Smart
products.verdict: A high-refresh set sized for smaller rooms.
products.description:
The 55 inch Hisense U7 is a Mini-LED ULED 4K set with a 165Hz panel, in the $500 and up bucket. Mini-LED backlights use many small LEDs, which allows better control of bright and dark areas than a conventional LED set. The 165Hz rate is the fastest in this ranking.

It earns third place because 55 inches is smaller than the TCL options, which limits it to a bedroom or small den. It is the right trade for gamers in a small room who want the top refresh rate without a giant screen.

Best for console and PC players. The caveat is that few video sources benefit from 165Hz. If you mostly watch movies, the TCL QM8K gives you a larger screen and gets the job done at 120Hz.

products.name: Hisense 85" U7 Mini-LED ULED 4K UHD Best Premium Gaming Smart Google
products.verdict: The biggest screen here, with the same 165Hz panel.
products.description:
The 85 inch Hisense U7 pairs Mini-LED ULED 4K with a 165Hz panel, in the $500 and up bucket. It is the largest screen in the ranking, aimed at a room that functions as a theater.

It lands fourth because it needs the most room, and the price rises accordingly compared with the 55 inch U7. An 85 inch set also weighs more than most households expect, and a delivery that cannot pass through a doorway is a bigger headache than a spec sheet.

It suits a dedicated home theater, with deep seating distance and a strong wall mount. Measure the wall and the doorways first, and check the weight rating of whatever will hold it. Skip it if space is short, because the 65 inch QM8K covers most rooms.

products.name: Hisense 65“ Hi-QLED S7 CanvasTV Series 4K UHD Google Smart Art TV
products.verdict: A TV that is meant to look like wall art when off.
products.description:
The Hisense CanvasTV S7 is a 65 inch Hi-QLED 4K set with a 144Hz panel, positioned as an art TV, in the $500 and up bucket. Art TVs aim to look like framed pictures when idle, so the television fades into decor instead of dominating the wall.

It sits fifth because its art focus is a style choice, not a picture-quality upgrade, and the listing gives few details about the art mode. The performance sets above give you the same 144Hz or better for similar money.

Choose it if looks matter as much as specs and the TV hangs in a living space you care about visually. Read the product page for art mode details before ordering, and skip it if you want the best picture per dollar.
products.skipIf: You want the best picture per dollar.

products.name: TCL 75 Inch Class QM6K Series
products.verdict: A large 75-inch 120Hz set in a lower series.
products.description:
The QM6K is a 75 inch TCL with a 120Hz panel, running Google TV, in the $500 and up bucket. It sits below the QM8 series in TCL's lineup and offers a large screen at a lower tier.

It ends the list because the listing gives the least detail on its panel. The spec line in our data reads OLED, which contradicts a mid-range series, so we do not trust it and leave panel type unverified. It does offer a large size at 120Hz, which keeps it relevant.

Best for buyers who want 75 inches without the QM8L's 144Hz. Verify the panel type on the product page before buying, and be wary of paying for a panel class the listing cannot confirm. The QM8K remains the safer pick.
products.idealFor: Large-room buyers on a tighter budget.

whatMatters.detail: A common rule is to sit roughly one and a half times the screen diagonal away for 4K. A 65 inch set suits about eight feet, an 85 inch about ten. Measure your couch distance before choosing, and leave room for the stand or mount. A screen too big for the room tires the eyes, and one too small wastes the resolution you paid for.

120Hz and above only help with sources that output that rate, such as consoles and PCs. Movies run at 24 frames, and streaming at even less. Check your console's output before paying for 144Hz or 165Hz, and match the panel to your highest-frame source, not to the headline number, because a faster panel adds cost without a visible gain on slower content.

QLED uses a quantum dot layer for color, while Mini-LED adds many small backlight zones for contrast. They solve different problems and can be combined. Look for the panel name in the listing title, and check the maker's page for zone counts, since the listings here omit them, and more zones generally gives finer contrast.

Google TV gives built-in streaming, voice search and a recommendation row across brands. The interface is the same on TCL and Hisense, so do not pay extra for it. Confirm the title says Google and not an alternative platform, because some similar models ship with different software, and the remote and apps will differ.

Large sets need space for the wall and the doorway. Check the product page for stand width and weight, and measure the route from the front door to the room. An 85 inch Hisense can be awkward to carry, and a mount must be rated for its weight, with an allowance for the stand legs and cables.

cards.label: 120Hz
cards.text: Plenty for sports and most consoles. Picks: TCL QM8K and TCL QM6K.

cards.label: 144Hz to 165Hz
cards.text: Matters for PC and high-refresh console play. Picks: TCL QM8L, Hisense CanvasTV S7 and both Hisense U7 sets.

cards.text: A 120Hz or higher panel and a size that fits your seating distance.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Hisense 55" U7 offers 165Hz in a small body, and the TCL QM8K is the balanced 120Hz choice.

cards.text: You game on PC or want a theater screen. The Hisense 85" U7 or TCL QM8L fit.

cards.text: You mostly stream. The TCL 75 Inch QM6K gives size without the top refresh rate.

faq.a: It is the smart TV platform built into these sets, offering streaming apps and voice search. The TCL and Hisense models all run it, so the interface is the same across the list, and your Google account carries between sets.

faq.q: What is a common buying mistake?
faq.a: Choosing the biggest screen without measuring the room. Check viewing distance first, because an 85 inch Hisense in a small living room is overwhelming, not cinematic, and forces you to turn your head to follow the action.

Only for gaming sources that output high refresh. For streaming and movies, 120Hz is enough, so the TCL QM8K covers most viewing. Buy 165Hz only if your console or PC can use it, and check that the TV's HDMI ports support the rate.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Plug in, connect to Wi-Fi and sign in with a Google account to download apps. The setup is the same across the TCL and Hisense sets and takes only a few minutes, mostly spent signing into apps.

faq.q: How do I care for the screen?
faq.a: Wipe with a dry microfiber cloth and avoid spraying liquid directly on it. Unplug the set first, and use light pressure so you do not press on the panel.

faq.q: Is the Google TV Streamer a TV?
faq.a: No, it is a streaming box. We kept this ranking to TV sets, so the Google TV Streamer was left out. It plugs into an existing TV to add the platform, so it only helps if you already own a screen.

finalTake: Buy the TCL 65 inch QM8K as the default Google TV for a living room. Take the QM8L for a big room with gaming sources, the 55 inch U7 for a small gaming room, and the 85 inch U7 only for a dedicated theater. Choose the CanvasTV when looks matter as much as specs. Measure first.
